title: A Hymn for the Well
premise: Lena Yarrow, a meticulous property surveyor, is sent to appraise Hollowell House before its sale — but the house documents her back, filling its ledgers with entries about her life she never wrote. As the harvest moon approaches, she discovers the previous owners invited something in through a ritual of hospitality, and it has been waiting for a guest who would stay past dark. The mirrors begin lagging one second behind reality, then begin showing rooms that don't exist. To survive until sunrise, Lena must choose between the house's offer of perfect belonging — a place that knows and keeps everything about her — and the truth that what was welcomed in must be named and refused aloud. She escapes at dawn by reading the house's own ledger back to it, un-inviting the invitation, though the final entry in her survey file is written in handwriting that isn't hers.
about_author: Jude Ashgrove is the pen name of a former rural land assessor who spent a decade cataloguing empty houses across the English countryside and swears three of them were occupied. They write horror about paperwork, property, and the terrible intimacy of places that remember.

chapters.title: The Commission
chapters.summary: Lena accepts an urgent appraisal of Hollowell House, a derelict estate whose sale must close before the harvest festival. Her POV establishes her creed: measure everything, document everything, trust nothing you can't file. The emotional beat is quiet professional pride shadowed by loneliness — she takes jobs like this because empty houses are easier than people.

chapters.title: Inventory
chapters.summary: Lena's first walkthrough: dust sheets, cold hearths, and a ledger on the hall table already bearing her name. POV stays with her as she catalogs anomalies as 'deferred maintenance.' The beat is unease rationalized into competence; she photographs the ledger and tells herself it's a seller's joke.

chapters.title: Square Footage
chapters.summary: Measuring day. Rooms return inconsistent dimensions — the east bedroom is four feet larger each time she measures it. Lena's POV, methodical, begins keeping a second private notebook. Emotional beat: the thrill of a puzzle, the first crack in her belief that anything can be filed into sense.

chapters.title: The Previous Owners
chapters.summary: In the village, Lena interviews the estate agent and an elderly neighbor, Mrs. Callow, who goes pale at the word 'guests.' She learns the Halloway family vanished mid-harvest, 1974, leaving dinner set for one extra. Beat: dread arriving sideways through small-town silence.

chapters.title: Entries Not Mine
chapters.summary: Back at the house, Lena finds her private notebook's contents copied into the house ledger — including thoughts she never wrote down. Whose POV blurs here: passages appear in first person she doesn't remember writing. Beat: violation; documentation, her prayer, has been answered by something else.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: The mirrors begin reflecting the room a beat behind. Lena tests them obsessively — stopwatch, candle, her own face smiling after she stops. Beat: terror of the self made slightly other; she realizes the lag is growing longer each hour.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: In the cellar, Lena finds the Halloways' ritual record: a rite of hospitality, bread and salt offered to 'the one who keeps the count,' meant to bind a guardian to the house. It worked. It stayed. Beat: horrified understanding — the entity isn't an intruder; it was welcomed, and hospitality binds both ways.

chapters.title: Locked In
chapters.summary: Dusk falls early. Doors open onto the same hallway; windows show the garden from yesterday. Lena's POV, claustrophobic, as her phone dies despite full charge. Beat: the shift from investigator to captive; her competence becomes the trap's mechanism.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Through the lagging mirror, the house speaks: stay, be known completely, belong perfectly — no more lonely motels, no more unreadable people. Lena, starving for belonging, nearly says yes. Beat: seduction; the horror offers exactly what she lacks.

chapters.title: Mrs. Callow's Warning
chapters.summary: A phone call that shouldn't connect: Mrs. Callow, herself once a guest who left, tells Lena the only exits — refuse the hospitality aloud before moonrise, or become part of the count forever. But refusal requires speaking the truth of what was invited, and the house will lie to stop her. Beat: fragile hope with a price attached.

chapters.title: Rooms That Don't Exist
chapters.summary: The house grows new rooms overnight: a nursery, a study with Lena's name carved in the desk, a kitchen where breakfast waits warm. Each room is tailored to a life she might have had. Beat: grief weaponized; the house shows her the belonging she never built.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: Lena finds the full ledger: every guest since 1740, each entry ending in a satisfied hand. The Halloways' page is unfinished — three names, blank fates. She understands she is being written into completion. Beat: existential dread; to be documented fully is to be finished.

chapters.title: Delay Tactics
chapters.summary: Lena fights for hours, sabotaging the house's rituals — salting thresholds, breaking mirrors, burning pages. The house repairs itself between heartbeats, and the mirror-lag stretches to ten seconds, showing her movements she hasn't made yet. Beat: desperate resistance meeting patient inevitability.

chapters.title: The Second Lena
chapters.summary: Her reflection steps out of sync entirely, moving independently, wearing the contentment Lena refused. It argues her case better than the house could: stay, rest, be loved by something that pays attention. Beat: the enemy becomes her own longing given a face.

chapters.title: Harvest Moonrise
chapters.summary: The moon rises red through every window at once. The house begins closing its count — doors becoming walls, the ledger opening to a fresh page bearing her name. Lena, cornered in the nursery that isn't hers, must find the truth to speak. Beat: point of no return.

chapters.title: The Truth of Hospitality
chapters.summary: Climax begins: Lena realizes the binding truth — the Halloways didn't invite a guardian, they invited a prisoner, offering false welcome to trap it. The entity's rage at betrayal powers the house. To free herself she must speak this truth aloud, siding with truth over the comfortable lie of belonging. Beat: moral pivot under mortal pressure.

chapters.title: Un-Invited
chapters.summary: Lena reads the Halloways' original deception from their own letters, voice steady, naming the crime: 'You were not welcomed. You were captured.' The house convulses; the ledger burns backward through centuries of stolen guests. Beat: cathartic reversal — her gift for documentation becomes the weapon.

chapters.title: Sunrise Terms
chapters.summary: The entity, freed of the false invitation, faces Lena directly — vast, ancient, and for the first time honest. It offers a true choice now, no lies. Lena refuses anyway: belonging bought even honestly isn't hers to take tonight. Beat: love against duty resolved; she chooses the hard world over the easy mirror.

chapters.title: Dawn Appraisal
chapters.summary: Gray light. The house stands ordinary, diminished, its impossible rooms folded away. Lena completes her survey with shaking hands, appraising Hollowell House at precisely its worth: unsellable. Beat: exhausted clarity; the professional ritual restored but changed forever.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Kept
chapters.summary: Before leaving, Lena reads the final pages: the freed guests' names, released at last, and one new entry — her own, closed with the word 'departed' in her handwriting. Some part of her remains counted. Beat: bittersweet cost; escape was real, but so was the marking.

chapters.title: Homesick
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Lena returns to her flat and her life, but mirrors everywhere lag — half a second, always half a second, only when she looks. She catches herself missing the house's attention. Beat: haunting aftermath; the wound of having been truly known.

chapters.title: A Hymn for the Well
chapters.summary: Final chapter: Lena writes her report, files it, and then writes a second document no client will see — a hymn, a warning, a welcome done properly this time, left in the village church for whoever inherits the problem. Last line reveals the well on Hollowell's grounds, long capped, humming. Beat: resolution with an open door; truth spoken, duty kept, and something below still listening.
